lines: Last topic's mechanism was correct. Open addressing really does keep every entry in the array itself.
But it still hops, one slot at a time, through its own probe sequence. This topic does the same kind of work in far fewer instructions.
Watch what happens when you stop asking 'is this one slot the right one' and start asking the same question of sixteen at once.
Two real costs, and Swiss Tables exist to avoid both of them.
A chained table pays a pointer and an allocation for every single entry. An open-addressed table avoids that, but its probe walk misses the cache on almost every step.
Keep both of those costs in mind. The next idea is built to dodge them at the same time.
Here's the setup. One group, sixteen slots, one control byte per slot.
Before I show you the real number, predict it yourself: how many of those sixteen does a single SIMD compare instruction actually test?
answer: All sixteen, in one instruction — Abseil's own design notes put it as 'winnowing sixteen candidates down... in only a few instructions.'
And it tests every one of them, occupied or not. The control byte is what decides afterward which lanes were even worth looking at.

lines: One hash value, doing two different jobs at once.
The larger share, H one, does what a hash always did: it picks which group to probe.
The smaller share, H two, gets a new job. It becomes that slot's own one byte fingerprint, stored separately from the key, right there in the control array.
Now sweep that fingerprint across the whole group's control bytes, all at once.
Almost every lane fades immediately — wrong fingerprint, ruled out with no key ever touched.
The one, maybe two, that match are the only candidates that earn a real comparison. That's the entire trick: reject almost everyone with one byte, before paying for the expensive check.
A seven-bit fingerprint has exactly a hundred and twenty-eight possible values.
Predict it: what are the odds a wrong candidate's fingerprint matches the query's by pure coincidence?
answer: About one in a hundred and twenty-eight — not nothing, which is exactly why a real key comparison still has to run whenever that one byte says 'maybe.'
The fingerprint isn't a replacement for the real check. It's just a filter good enough that you almost never pay for one.

lines: I didn't just take that one-in-a-hundred-twenty-eight number on faith — I measured it, directly, in this topic's own code.
Twenty thousand lookups for keys that were never inserted, and the rate the false matches actually land at tracks the theoretical odds closely.
That's the whole design in one sentence: the fingerprint doesn't replace the real comparison, it just makes paying for one incredibly rare.
Three real languages and runtimes, and I went and checked each one myself, not from memory.
Abseil's own C++ design, from twenty seventeen, open-sourced the following year. Rust's standard library HashMap, through the hashbrown crate, since a version released years back.
And Go's built-in map, adopted this very year — a current blog post is what I actually fetched for that one, not an older version I remembered.
One mechanism, three independent adopters, each one verified at research time.

And the asymmetry that makes it all worth it, measured, not asserted: on a packed group, the vectorized compare still costs one instruction. A naive, byte-by-byte scan of that same group costs sixteen.
Same correctness. Sixteen times fewer instructions to get there.
